label: Motion Planning
notes: This chapter, printed pages 353 to 402, reframes robot motion as a search for a point through configuration space rather than a body through workspace. We preview the planning question, the free-versus-forbidden split, and the family of complete, grid, sampling, and optimization methods that answer it.

label: The Path-Planning Problem
notes: We state the problem precisely: given a start configuration, a goal, and a collision model, return a continuous path lying entirely in free space, or report failure. Every later method is just a different policy for searching this same object, so naming it early keeps the chapter organized.

label: Configuration-Space Obstacles
notes: A collision checker maps each candidate configuration to a yes or no verdict, splitting C-space into free and obstacle regions. The key lesson is that a simple workspace obstacle can carve a twisted, high-dimensional forbidden region, which is exactly why planning is hard and why we plan with points.

label: Planning a Collision-Free Path
notes: Here the abstraction pays off: a robot body weaving past a table becomes a single point tracing a curve around a C-obstacle blob. We trace start to goal through the free region and stress that membership in free space, not visual neatness, is the invariant every planner must preserve.

label: Three Families of Planners
notes: We organize methods into complete, grid, and sampling families, each trading guarantees against cost. Complete planners promise an answer but scale poorly; grids are resolution complete; sampling planners are probabilistically complete. Knowing which guarantee a method offers tells you when a failure is the method's fault or the resolution's fault.

label: Graph Search: A* and Dijkstra
notes: Once a roadmap or grid exists, planning becomes shortest-path search. Dijkstra expands by accumulated cost; A* adds an admissible heuristic that never overestimates remaining distance, so it stays optimal while exploring fewer nodes. The admissibility condition is the load-bearing assumption behind that optimality claim.

label: Grid-Based Search and Wavefront
notes: A grid planner discretizes C-space, marks blocked cells, and runs a wavefront flood from the goal so every free cell stores its distance-to-goal. Following decreasing values yields a path. It is resolution complete: a corridor narrower than the grid spacing can vanish between samples, so the planner may confidently solve the wrong problem.

label: Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM)
notes: PRM samples free configurations, connects nearby ones with a local planner into a reusable roadmap, then answers many queries by graph search. It excels in high dimensions where grids are hopeless, but narrow passages stay hard because random samples rarely land in tightly constrained regions of free space.

label: Rapidly-Exploring Random Trees
notes: RRT grows a single tree rooted at the start. Each step samples a target, finds the nearest tree node, and extends a short step toward it, biasing growth into unexplored regions. It is single-query and probabilistically complete; RRT* rewires neighbors so the path cost converges toward optimal as samples increase.

label: Virtual Potential Fields
notes: Potential fields treat the goal as an attractive well and obstacles as repulsive hills; the robot descends the combined gradient. The motion looks smooth and reactive, but superimposed fields can create spurious local minima that trap the robot short of the goal, which is the method's defining failure mode.

label: Nonlinear Optimization Planning
notes: Optimization planning casts the path as decision variables and minimizes a cost subject to collision and dynamic constraints. It can fold smoothness, clearance, and actuator limits into one objective, but the program is nonconvex, so solvers need good initial guesses and may settle into local optima rather than the global best path.

label: Smoothing and Takeaways
notes: Smoothing comes after feasibility: it shortens or regularizes a jagged feasible path while re-checking clearance and dynamic limits, since the protected invariant is free-space membership, not visual smoothness. The chapter's thesis is that planning equals geometry plus a search policy, and resolution and sampling choices are part of the model.
